name: HGH for height

card.summary: Using growth hormone to try to grow taller; studied in children with short stature, with modest gains, and untested for healthy adults with closed growth plates.
card.aka: growth hormone for height, somatropin, GH, hGH-for-height
card.note: Prescription-only; trials are in children with growth plates open. Evidence for height gain in healthy adults is not available, and long-term risks in healthy adults are described as unknown.

quick.overview:
Human growth hormone (HGH, somatropin) is a prescription injectable used medically for growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, small-for-gestational-age short stature and several other conditions. 'HGH for height' refers to using it, medically or non-medically, to increase height in someone who is short for reasons other than a hormone deficiency, or to try for extra height in the looksmaxxing context.

In clinical trials of children with idiopathic short stature, treatment over several years has been reported to add a few centimetres of adult height on average. Paediatric endocrinology papers debate whether this is meaningful, call it 'cosmetic endocrinology' and discuss cost and ethics. On forums, some users who are past their teenage years ask whether HGH can still add height; no clinical trial identified for this article tests that.
quick.mechanism: Growth hormone acts on the liver and tissues to raise IGF-1 and stimulates growth at the growth plates in the long bones of children and adolescents. Height gain requires open growth plates; after the plates fuse, bones cannot lengthen from growth stimulation. Forum users also talk about growth-hormone-releasing peptides and IGF-1 analogues as alternatives, which are separate and largely unstudied for this purpose.
quick.risks: Documented effects of growth hormone therapy include reduced insulin sensitivity, and some cancer-subgroup signals in large studies. A 2003 editorial cautioned against off-label use and noted that long-term risks in healthy adults are unknown. Forum users report changes such as a widening nose, and cost can be very high. Growth hormone is a prescription drug in most countries, and counterfeit or mislabelled products have been reported in the gray market.

lead: Human growth hormone (HGH), or somatropin, is a peptide hormone made by the pituitary gland and sold as a recombinant prescription drug. 'HGH for height' means using it to increase stature: medically, in children whose growth is impaired by deficiency or by conditions such as Turner syndrome, and in children who are short without a known cause; and, in looksmaxxing communities, by teenagers and young adults who hope to add inches beyond where they expect to finish [1][2][10]. Added height is one of the most direct appearance payoffs a medical treatment can claim, because stature changes how proportions, presence and photographs read at every angle.

Growth hormone lengthens bones by acting at the growth plates, the cartilage zones at the ends of long bones, both directly and through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) made mainly in the liver [12][17]. Because plates fuse during or shortly after puberty, the treatment trials that report height gains are in children and adolescents; reported median gains are roughly 5 to 8 cm in Turner syndrome and 4 to 8 cm in extreme idiopathic short stature after about four years of treatment [1]. Wikipedia's short stature article gives a typical addition of about 5 to 10 cm to adult height from therapy, over years of injections [21].

Pediatric endocrinology journals describe extending treatment to children without a hormone deficiency as 'cosmetic endocrinology' and debate its cost, ethics and effect on wellbeing [3][4]. No clinical trial has tested growth hormone for height in healthy adults whose growth plates have closed, and a 2003 pair of New England Journal of Medicine editorials, summarized by Wikipedia, said safety and efficacy in healthy adults had not been established [1]. Forum posters ask about using it anyway, often with releasing peptides and IGF-1 analogues, which are separate compounds [9][10][11].

chain: Recombinant growth hormone raises circulating GH and IGF-1
Growth-plate cartilage and long bones grow faster while plates are open
Adult height ends up higher than it otherwise would have been in the conditions studied
angle.text: In children with open growth plates and certain diagnoses, growth hormone injections raise growth velocity and add a few centimetres of adult height. Looksmaxxing posters ask whether the same applies after puberty, a use no trial has tested.

paras: Somatropin is a 191-amino-acid peptide made by somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary and released in pulses, with the largest peak about an hour after sleep onset and nearly half of daily secretion in deep sleep. Secretion is higher in adolescents (about 700 micrograms a day) than in healthy adults (about 400) [12]. The hormone has a half-life of 10 to 20 minutes in blood, so therapeutic forms are given by injection [12]. Brands include Humatrope, Genotropin, Norditropin, Nutropin, Saizen and Zomacton, plus once-weekly products Sogroya and Skytrofa [1][19].

Height depends on open growth plates. Wikipedia describes plate fusion as complete in girls as early as 12 with 14 to 15 most common, and in boys as early as 14 with 15 to 17 most common, with some studies reporting most males finishing by about 19; rising estrogen triggers programmed death of the plate's cartilage cells and the plate is replaced by bone [17]. When excess growth hormone begins in childhood, before the plates close, the result is gigantism; after closure, it produces acromegaly, with enlargement of hands, feet, jaw, brow, nose and lips rather than added height [18].

Growth hormone therapy is approved for growth hormone deficiency in children and adults and for growth failure in Turner syndrome, chronic kidney failure, Prader-Willi syndrome (children), intrauterine growth retardation and short-stature homeobox gene deficiency [1][19]. It was approved for AIDS-related wasting in adults in 2004, and for idiopathic short stature in 2003 [1].

Idiopathic short stature (ISS) is extreme short height with no cause found after routine evaluation; the term has been used since at least 1975 and has no precise statistical definition [2]. In 2003 Eli Lilly proposed height more than 2.25 standard deviations below the mean, about the shortest 1.2 percent, as the threshold, and some researchers use 2.0 standard deviations [2]. Wikipedia reports that trial participants had predicted adult heights under 160 cm for boys and 150 cm for girls, and notes critics' point that many of the children had low IGF-1 levels [1].

For short stature, treatment aims to move a child toward or into the typical range of adult height. Reviews in Hormone Research in Paediatrics describe 'hGH-for-height' as arising from assumptions that short stature is a disability that treatment can improve, and report modest and variable benefit [3][4]. Short stature is defined by Wikipedia as roughly two standard deviations below the mean, and the same article notes that most very short adults are not physically or psychologically disabled by height, while some evidence links lower height to other disadvantages [21].

Outside prescribed use, posters on looksmax.org describe taking or considering growth hormone in their late teens, sometimes after using releasing peptides without seeing height change, hoping that growth plates remain open [10]. Height gain after plate closure is not a documented effect of therapy; the plate-closure literature says longitudinal growth ends when the cartilage has been replaced by bone [17].

Cosmetic limb lengthening is a surgical route: bones of the legs are cut and gradually separated with an external or implanted device while new bone forms. Wikipedia traces the technique to proposals in 1869, early clinical work by Codivilla in 1905 and Ilizarov's work from the 1950s, and describes high demand and little regulation in India, a 2006 ban in China, and complication rates including infection in about 5 percent of cases [20]. Wikipedia's short stature article also mentions IGF-1 and aromatase inhibitors as proposed alternatives to growth hormone [2][21].

A randomized trial in 40 girls with Turner syndrome found that height velocity rose from about 3.8 cm per year before treatment to roughly 7.5 to 8 cm per year during the first year of growth hormone with or without low-dose oestrogen [5]. Encyclopedia summaries give median adult height gains of roughly 5 to 8 cm in Turner syndrome and 4 to 8 cm in extreme ISS, and note that in chronic kidney failure treatment may narrow a height deficit while a deficit of around 10 cm can remain [1].

Authors in Hormone Research in Paediatrics describe the benefit in children who are short for reasons other than deficiency as modest and variable, and argue that cost-conscious practice is possible because it is hard to measure the therapeutic effect [3][4]. Wikipedia reports that treatment may not significantly improve psychosocial functioning and puts costs at $100,000 or more per person for a move from about the first to the tenth percentile [2], and gives costs of about $20,000 a year for a small child and over $50,000 for a teenager [21].

Registered trials include a study in 115 young girls with Turner syndrome treated before age 4 [13], a phase 3 trial of Saizen in 90 children with idiopathic short stature [6], a phase 3 trial in 91 children born with serious intrauterine growth retardation [7] and a pharmaco-epidemiological study in 150 short children born small for gestational age [16]. A 2021 study compared weekly and daily growth hormone schedules on quality of life in short children using the QoLISSY questionnaire [14].

Growth hormone acts through receptors on target cells; the MAPK/ERK pathway directly stimulates cartilage cell division, and the JAK-STAT pathway drives the liver to produce IGF-1, which promotes bone growth through osteoblasts and chondrocytes [12]. Estrogen and androgens, fasting, deep sleep and vigorous exercise are described as influences on secretion, and high GH or IGF-1 and high blood sugar as inhibitors [12].

Growth-hormone-releasing peptides and releasing hormone act upstream, prompting the pituitary to release its own hormone, and are discussed on forums as alternatives to injecting somatropin [10][12]. Long-acting weekly formulations were approved in the US in 2020 and 2021 [1].

Growth hormone therapy usually reduces insulin sensitivity, though some studies found no clear rise in diabetes among adults treated for hypopituitarism [1]. A study of 6,840 treated adults found no overall rise in primary cancer, with higher risk in some subgroups such as patients under 35 and those with childhood-onset deficiency; the FDA's 2011 safety communication called evidence on death risk inconclusive, and a small trial in critically ill adults found higher mortality [1]. Joint swelling and pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and a possible link to Hodgkin's lymphoma are also listed with therapeutic use [12].

Prolonged excess of the hormone from a pituitary tumour causes acromegaly: a protruding lower jaw with widened tooth spacing, prominent brow, larger nose and lips, thickened skin, joint pain, diabetes, sleep apnea, heart enlargement and reduced life expectancy if untreated [18]. A looksmax.org poster who reported a widened nose after over a year of use at 5 foot 8 asked whether to continue, and replies raised suppression of natural production [9]. Wikipedia's account of the cadaver-derived era records Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in 26 recipients treated before 1977 [1].

Animal growth hormone did not work in humans. In the late 1950s Maurice Raben purified enough from human pituitaries to treat a deficient boy, and in 1960 the National Pituitary Agency was formed under the NIH to collect pituitaries at autopsy and distribute the hormone; between 1963 and 1985 about 7,700 US children and 27,000 worldwide received it, under rationing [1]. In 1985, after four young adults who had received it developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, pituitary hormone was withdrawn, and Genentech's recombinant Protropin was introduced at roughly $10,000 to $30,000 per year, after trials begun in 1981 [1][19].

In the 1990s Eli Lilly's trials in children at least 2.25 standard deviations below the mean reported gains of about 4 to 8 cm; the FDA approved Humatrope for ISS in 2003, a controversial decision that Wikipedia says increased demand for treating otherwise normal children [1][2]. Wikipedia's short stature article says critics have alleged that manufacturers promoted short stature as a disease through funded height-screening programs [21].

Outside pediatrics, a 1990 study of men over 60 by Rudman and Ronald Klatz's 1997 book brought growth hormone to a general audience as an anti-aging therapy; 2003 editorials cautioned about off-label use and 'HGH-releasing' supplements, and Wikipedia notes scams associated with the label and gym-circulated fraudulent products [1].

In the United States recombinant growth hormone is available legally only by prescription; Wikipedia says a 1990 law made distributing it for non-medical use a felony, that a 2015 DEA position treats off-label prescribing as illegal, and that the FDA says it does not regulate off-label use [12]. Anti-aging clinic use in older adults has not been tested in trials for efficacy and safety [12]. Athletes have used it since at least 1982 and the IOC and NCAA ban it [12].

Authors in Hormone Research in Paediatrics describe 'cosmetic endocrinology' as treatment of normal variation and discuss cost, fairness and the assumption that short stature is a disability, recommending restraint and informed assent [3][4]. Wikipedia notes concern that treatment could shift disadvantage to the next shortest percentile [2].

On looksmax.org, threads include an 18-year-old at 5 foot 10 asking whether to move from releasing peptides to growth hormone and IGF-1 LR3 to gain an inch without knowing his plate status [10], a poster asking how to schedule and administer it, with replies reflecting personal experience rather than clinical guidance [11], and a user weighing height against a widening nose [9]. Height is a prominent topic in the wider scene alongside surgical limb lengthening, which Wikipedia says has been sought in India for marriage and career reasons [20].

Controlled trials exist in children, including a randomized trial of growth hormone with and without oestrogen in Turner syndrome [5], a phase 3 trial of Saizen in 90 children with idiopathic short stature [6], a phase 3 trial in 91 children born with serious intrauterine growth retardation [7] and a not-yet-recruiting phase 3 trial of a Chinese growth hormone injection in ISS [8]. Further registered studies include a phase 3 trial in 105 children born small for gestational age [15] and a 150-patient study of Saizen in short children born small for gestational age [16]. Review papers evaluate cost-effectiveness and ethics of 'hGH-for-height' [3][4].
No studies found of growth hormone for height gain in healthy adults with fused growth plates.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, growth hormone is discussed as a possible way to gain extra height or to keep growing into the late teens, often alongside releasing peptides and IGF-1 analogues [9][10][11].

claims.claim: HGH can still add height even if you are past puberty.
claims.believers: Posters in their late teens ask whether it is too late to add an inch, and some replies say you might still grow while others say height gain is not possible [10].
claims.experts: Controlled trials of growth hormone for height are in children with open growth plates; no clinical trial has tested it in healthy adults, and plates are generally reported to fuse by about 19 [1][5][6][17].

claims.claim: Growth-hormone-releasing peptides (CJC-1295, ipamorelin) or IGF-1 LR3 can substitute for HGH for height.
claims.believers: One user reports using a releasing-peptide combination for about six weeks without noticeable benefit and asks about moving to HGH and IGF-1 LR3, which a reply recommends [10].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested these peptides or analogues for height gain in healthy people; Wikipedia describes releasing peptides as acting on the pituitary to prompt its own release [12].

claims.claim: HGH causes facial changes such as a wider nose.
claims.believers: A user reports that his nose became wide after over a year of use and weighs continuing for height against facial change [9].
claims.experts: Enlargement of the nose, lips, jaw and brow is documented in acromegaly, caused by prolonged growth hormone excess after plate closure; facial changes are not listed as a standard effect of pediatric dosing [18][1].

claims.claim: There is a right way to cycle HGH (on/off schedules, subcutaneous versus intramuscular).
claims.believers: Users trade schedules they have seen and say subcutaneous seems to work better [11].
claims.experts: Clinical dosing is individualized by prescribers; no published trial evaluates cycling schedules for height in healthy people [1].

claims.claim: Using natural stimulation, such as releasing peptides or sleep, can protect natural GH while using synthetic.
claims.believers: A reply suggests raw milk and GH peptides to spur natural production while synthetic hormone is depleting it [9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes GH release as pulsatile, peaking after sleep onset, with deep sleep and vigorous exercise as stimulators and high GH or IGF-1 as negative feedback; no trial tests this combination for height [12].

claims.claim: Giving growth hormone to normal short children is 'cosmetic endocrinology'.
claims.believers: This is the position of some pediatric endocrinology authors, who recommend restraint in enhancing normal adult stature [3][4].
claims.experts: Reviews call the benefit modest and variable and discuss ethics, cost and fairness; Wikipedia reports FDA approval for ISS in 2003 [2][3][4].
